case_study_insert.main_stem: Wexley Plasterboard (WPB) is a private limited company in the building materials sector, employing a workforce of 85. Founded in 2011 by Priya Wexley, the business manufactures gypsum plasterboard with recycled-paper facings for the construction industry and operates a hierarchical organisational structure with autocratic leadership. WPB plans to invest $1,400,000 in a new automated drying and cutting line, financed by a $900,000 ten-year bank loan and $500,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $600,000 a year, a variable cost of $7.50 a unit and a selling price of $12.50, and currently produces 170,000 units a year. WPB faces two operational problems: a board defect rate of 2.6% with rising cutting-line waste, and labour turnover among machine operators has reached 14%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Report — Q3 2025: The drying line produced 44,000 boards in the quarter at a defect rate of 2.6%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 30 to 16 per month. Market research of 480 builders' merchants found that 71% would stock certified low-carbon plasterboard and 58% would pay up to $0.60 more per sheet. Average delivery time is 4 days and cutting waste is running at 6.5% of output. A training needs analysis shows 18 of 85 staff have not completed on-the-job training on the new saws; off-the-job training courses at the technical college cost $750 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Wexley Plasterboard for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.25% to 4.75%, the third rise this year, lifting borrowing costs on variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.9% from $11.40 to $12.07 per hour from April 2026, raising total wage bills. (3) Gypsum and recycled paper input costs have risen 9.8% year-on-year, and construction-materials inflation is running at 7.3%, while housing starts grew 3.2% in the same period.

questions.question_text: WPB plans to finance part of its automated drying and cutting line expansion with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for WPB of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using retained profit costs WPB nothing in interest or repayment charges, which protects cash flow at a time when the company already carries fixed costs of $600,000 a year and has committed to a $900,000 ten-year bank loan for the $1,400,000 automated drying and cutting line. Avoiding interest on the retained $500,000 leaves more operating cash to absorb the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs, so WPB can defend its $12.50 selling price against cheaper imports and keep the 2.6% defect-reduction programme funded without straining merchant order books.

Point 2: Retained profit avoids the collateral and repayment risk attached to a bank loan, so the $500,000 is available without putting the new $1,400,000 line at risk of repossession if construction demand disappoints. It also preserves Priya Wexley's ownership and control of the private limited company, since no lender can impose covenants or conditions on how the automated line is operated, priced or expanded in later phases — particularly valuable while housing starts are only growing 3.2% a year.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Wexley Plasterboard and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: WPB is launching its recycled-paper plasterboard range. Consider national trade-press advertising, regional radio sponsorship, or social media influencer marketing aimed at builders. Which should WPB choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National trade-press advertising: Full-page adverts in construction and builders' merchant journals would reach procurement officers and merchant owners nationally with a credible technical message about certified low-carbon board. However, colour space is expensive, the readership is broad — much of it is architects or DIY readers outside WPB's merchant coverage — and a single insertion gives no measurable response data, making it hard to judge against a tight launch budget on top of an $900,000 loan commitment.

Regional radio sponsorship: Sponsoring a drive-time building programme is far cheaper than national print and would reach site managers and merchant staff commuting across WPB's Derbyshire catchment with high frequency. Its weakness is narrow geographic reach: WPB supplies merchant chains nationally and wants the 71% of surveyed merchants who would stock certified low-carbon plasterboard to hear the message everywhere, not just regionally. Radio also struggles to convey technical performance such as facing strength and defect rates.

Social media influencer marketing: Working with builders, joiners and sustainable-construction influencers targets exactly the 58% of 480 surveyed merchants willing to pay $0.60 more per sheet and the 71% planning to stock low-carbon board. Cost per reached buyer is low, engagement and click-throughs are measurable, and influencers can demonstrate the recycled-paper facing story on real sites — ideal for a technical B2B product. Credibility depends on honest, experienced voices rather than celebrities.

Recommendation: WPB should choose social media influencer marketing. It reaches the precise segments already identified in its research, scales nationally, produces measurable results and costs far less than trade press or radio, fitting a company servicing debt on a $900,000 loan. National trade-press advertising is rejected as too expensive and insufficiently targeted for launch; regional radio is rejected as too narrow for national merchant listings. WPB should nevertheless support influencers with modest in-store merchant promotions to capture older buyers who do not use social media.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of WPB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of WPB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why trade press and radio are rejected.

questions.question_text: WPB's labour turnover among machine operators has reached 14% under autocratic leadership. Explain two benefits for WPB of using appraisal to improve operator performance.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Appraisal gives each of WPB's 85 employees a formal review of performance against clear standards, identifying the 18 staff who have not completed on-the-job training on the new saws and linking them to targeted training at $750 per employee. This directly attacks the 2.6% defect rate and 6.5% cutting waste, reducing rework costs on the drying line and protecting the 44,000 boards produced last quarter without adding overtime or rushing new operators onto the $1,400,000 automated line before they are competent.

Point 2: Appraisal recognises operators' strengths and effort, giving them esteem and a sense of progress (Maslow) that offsets the frustration of autocratic leadership. Higher morale should reduce the 14% labour turnover, cutting recruitment and induction costs and the risk that half-trained operators leave with hard-won skills. Stable staffing keeps the 170,000-unit output target achievable and supports Priya Wexley's plan to justify the expansion to the bank.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WPB's labour turnover, defects, training and output.

questions.question_text: WPB must upskill 18 operators for the new automated drying and cutting line. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the technical college at $750 per employee. Which should WPB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training operators at the drying line is directly relevant to WPB's own saws, board sizes and recycled-paper facings, costs nothing in course fees beyond the trainer's time, and keeps the 18 staff productive while they learn — protecting the 44,000 boards produced last quarter and the effort behind the fall from 4.0% to 2.6% defects. Its weaknesses are that operators learn from production colleagues who may pass on bad habits, structured theory (board moisture science, waste minimisation) is limited, and no external certificate is issued to show merchants or auditors.

Off-the-job training: College courses at $750 per employee would cost $13,500 for all 18 — affordable against an $1,400,000 investment. They give structured, up-to-date content and recognised certificates, which strengthens WPB's quality claims to certified stockists. However, it removes 18 of 85 staff (over a fifth of the workforce) from the line for course days, risking delivery slips, and generic content may not match WPB's exact machine settings, so follow-up coaching on site would still be needed.

Decision: WPB should choose on-the-job training for the initial rollout, with two or three lead operators sent to college for certification. This is cheapest, machine-specific and avoids further output loss while turnover is 14% and waste is 6.5%; margins must stay intact to service the $900,000 loan. Full off-the-job training is rejected because withholding $13,500 is not the issue — removing a fifth of production capacity is, and the college curriculum would not address recycled-facing handling. WPB can add college visits for senior operators once the line stabilises and defects fall below 2.0%.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to WPB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of WPB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of WPB with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how WPB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $600,000 ÷ ($12.50 − $7.50) = $600,000 ÷ $5.00 = 120,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 120,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $12.50 − $7.50 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways WPB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. WPB's managers can compare the 120,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 170,000 units, confirming the plant is comfortably profitable with a margin of safety of 50,000 units, and decide whether to ramp the new automated line towards full capacity.
2. Contribution per unit of $5.00 lets managers model a negotiated discount, for example a 4% price cut to $12.00 would drop contribution to $4.50, letting them judge whether extra volume would still cover the $600,000 fixed costs before signing national merchant contracts.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $600,000 and contribution per unit helps managers set the volume targets used to service the $900,000 bank loan, checking the $1,400,000 expansion can generate the cash for repayments before committing any further capital.
4. Managers can use unit cost data ($600,000 ÷ 170,000 units + $7.50 = $11.03 a unit) to benchmark performance across quarters, pinpoint waste driving the 6.5% cutting-line losses, and decide whether to renegotiate the $7.50 variable cost with gypsum suppliers amid the 9.8% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 120,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 50,000 units against 170,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $600,000 fixed costs; bank-loan and $1,400,000 expansion feasibility; and unit-cost benchmarking at $11.03 to tackle 2.6% defects and 6.5% cutting waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate WPB's profitability by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has WPB's profitability improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.5%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 17.5%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit = $8,400,000 revenue − $5,040,000 cost of sales = $3,360,000; 2025 gross profit = $9,600,000 − $5,280,000 = $4,320,000. 2024 operating profit of $1,050,000 ÷ revenue of $8,400,000 = 12.5%; 2025 operating profit of $1,440,000 ÷ revenue of $9,600,000 = 15.0%. 2024 operating profit of $1,050,000 ÷ capital employed of $6,000,000 = 17.5%; 2025 operating profit of $1,440,000 ÷ capital employed of $7,200,000 = 20.0%. Revenue grew $1,200,000 while cost of sales rose only $240,000, so gross profit rose $960,000 year-on-year.

Evaluation: Profitability has clearly strengthened. Gross profit rose from $3,360,000 to $4,320,000 because revenue grew much faster than cost of sales — evidence that the certified low-carbon board mix and the $0.60 per-sheet premium are working. Operating profit rose 37% to $1,440,000, outpacing revenue growth of about 14%. Capital employed grew $1,200,000 to fund the cutting line, yet returns on that capital still rose from 17.5% to 20.0%, showing the expansion is earning comfortably above its financing cost even though interest payable rose from $120,000 to $150,000 on the $900,000 loan. Risks remain: the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs could compress the improved margins if WPB cannot pass them on, and 14% labour turnover adds $750-per-head retraining costs that trim operating profit.

Conclusion: WPB's profitability has improved. Gross profit, operating profit and the return on capital employed all rose in 2025, and the improvement is broad-based rather than dependent on one-off factors. The main residual risks are debt servicing at higher interest rates and operator turnover, so WPB should lock in supplier contracts and complete the defect-reduction programme before committing further capital.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether WPB's profitability improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for WPB of producing its plasterboard with recycled-paper facings instead of virgin-paper facings.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recycled-paper facings match the 58% of 480 surveyed builders' merchants willing to pay up to $0.60 more per sheet for certified low-carbon board, letting WPB charge a premium that protects its $5.00 contribution per unit even as gypsum and recycled paper input costs rise 9.8%. It also satisfies the 71% of merchants planning to stock certified low-carbon plasterboard, strengthening WPB's brand with housebuilders chasing their own sustainability targets and supporting the case for the $1,400,000 expansion.

Disadvantage: Recycled facing supply can be inconsistent in moisture content and strength, raising the risk of delamination and pushing the 2.6% defect rate and 6.5% cutting waste back up before the new automated drying line stabilises. If merchants will not pay the $0.60 premium nationally, WPB could be left with a higher variable cost than $7.50 and no compensating revenue — squeezing margins and weakening the returns needed to service the $900,000 bank loan.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to WPB's research data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 4.75%, the 5.9% minimum wage increase and the 9.8% rise in gypsum and recycled paper input costs will affect WPB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.25% to 4.75%): If WPB's $900,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by about 0.5%, adding roughly $4,500 a year — small beside fixed costs of $600,000. Higher rates also raise the hurdle for any future phase of the $1,400,000 expansion and may cool housing starts (already only growing 3.2%), but the direct cash impact is modest and WPB could negotiate a fixed rate at renewal.

Minimum wage increase (5.9%, to $12.07 per hour): Only a minority of WPB's 85 staff sit at or near the minimum wage, mostly production operatives on the drying line. For around 40 production staff, the increase adds about $0.67 an hour, or roughly $1,400 per worker a year — about $56,000 across the affected group. Manageable, but it will press on margins if WPB cannot raise prices above $12.50, and democratic input (or at least better appraisal feedback) would help contain the 14% turnover it worsens.

Input cost inflation (9.8% gypsum and recycled paper): Ingredients dominate the $7.50 variable cost; assume roughly 70% ($5.25) is materials. A 9.8% rise adds about $0.51 per unit; at 170,000 units that is roughly $87,000 a year, cutting contribution from $5.00 to about $4.49 and reducing annual profit by around 14% if not passed on. WPB can recover part through the $0.60 eco-premium and merchant price reviews, but not all, since 71% of merchants will resist across-the-board rises.

Conclusion: The 9.8% input cost rise will have the greatest impact. It recurs on every one of the 170,000 units sold, eroding the $5.00 contribution directly and totalling roughly $85,000–$90,000 a year — well above the wage rise (~$56,000) and the loan interest increase (~$4,500). The wage rise is the second most serious threat, while the rate rise is the least damaging and easiest to hedge; all three nevertheless demand supplier contracts, premium pricing and tighter cost control to protect the expansion's returns.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to WPB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on WPB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of WPB with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
